# Distributed Systems in Practice: A Reference for Senior Backend Engineers

## Introduction

Most backend engineers meet distributed systems through an incident. A write succeeds on one node and disappears after a failover. Two services disagree about a balance and neither is obviously wrong. A timeout fires, the client retries, and the customer is charged twice. These failures are rarely caused by ignorance of any single algorithm. They come from holding several partial truths at once: that networks drop and delay messages, that clocks drift, that processes pause for garbage collection or get descheduled, and that a node which looks dead may be alive and still acting on old information.

This guide is for engineers who already build and operate networked services and want a precise, working model of how distributed systems behave. It assumes you know concurrency, can read a database's isolation documentation, and have written code that talks over HTTP or gRPC. It does not assume you have implemented consensus or read the original papers, though it points to them where they matter.

The guide is written as a sequence of sections, one per message, over a long session. Each section takes one topic and works it to the level of mechanism: what the problem is, what the common solutions guarantee, what they cost, and how they fail. The planned arc runs roughly as follows. We begin with the failure model: partial failure, asynchronous networks, timeouts, and the impossibility results that constrain every later choice. Next come time and ordering, covering clock skew, logical clocks, and why "happened before" is the right notion of causality. From there we move to replication and consistency, including leader-based and leaderless designs, quorums, and the spectrum from linearizability to eventual consistency. Then consensus: how a group of nodes agrees on a sequence of decisions, and how that agreement is used to build a replicated log and membership changes. Transactions follow, covering atomic commitment across partitions, the limits of two-phase commit, and the practical tradeoffs in isolation. The later sections address idempotency and exactly-once effects, backpressure and overload, failure detection, and operational concerns such as observability, rolling upgrades, and testing under fault injection.

### Our running example: Kestrel

Every worked example in this guide uses Kestrel, a payments ledger. Kestrel records debits and credits against customer accounts and must never lose a committed entry, never apply the same payment twice, and never let an account balance go negative under a valid rule set. Those requirements make it a useful stress test, because each property constrains a different part of the design.

Kestrel runs on 5 nodes spread across 3 regions, which we will call `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-south`. The placement is 2 nodes in `us-east`, 2 in `eu-west`, and 1 in `ap-south`. This layout is deliberate. With 5 nodes, a majority is 3, so any operation that needs a majority can proceed while any 2 nodes are unavailable. If either 2-node region is cut off entirely, the remaining 3 nodes still form a majority. If the single `ap-south` node is lost, Kestrel continues without interruption. The cost is that a majority quorum usually spans at least two regions, so every committed write pays cross-region latency. That tradeoff, between availability under regional loss and write latency, is one we will return to repeatedly.

Kestrel is not a toy. Its numbers are chosen to be realistic: payments writes are on the order of a few thousand per second at peak, account balances are read far more often than they are written, and a single payment touches at most two accounts. Where a section needs a simpler model, we will say so explicitly and then return to Kestrel's actual layout.

### Conventions

Code examples are in Go and are written to be compiled and reasoned about, not merely skimmed. They favor explicit error handling, `context.Context` for cancellation and deadlines, and standard library primitives where possible. When an example shows a failure, it shows the failure path in the code, not just the happy path.

Terminology is kept strict. A server in a cluster is a node. We use "leader" and "follower" only as roles a node can hold at a given moment, not as separate kinds of machine. When a section discusses a set of nodes that hold the same data, it will say so in those terms.

Each section ends with a single summary line. Read those lines in sequence and you have the guide's argument in compressed form; read the sections and you have the reasoning behind each line.

Key takeaway: Distributed systems fail in ways that single-machine intuition does not predict, so this guide builds a precise model of partial failure, time, and agreement, then tests every technique against one concrete system, Kestrel, so its costs and failure modes are visible rather than abstract.

# Consensus Algorithms: The Mechanisms That Matter

Consensus lets a set of nodes agree on a single sequence of decisions even when some nodes crash and messages are lost, delayed, or reordered. Raft, Paxos, and Zab solve the same core problem with different vocabularies. Once you see past the names, the same six mechanisms recur. Each one exists to protect a specific safety property, and each has a failure mode that shows up in production.

Kestrel, our payments ledger, runs on 5 nodes: 2 in `us-east`, 2 in `eu-west`, and 1 in `ap-south`. A majority is 3. The examples below use that layout.

## 1. Terms, Ballots, and Epochs

Every consensus protocol needs a way to order leadership attempts. Raft calls these numbers **terms**, Paxos calls them **ballot numbers** (proposal numbers), and Zab calls them **epochs**. Each leadership attempt gets a number strictly greater than any previous one, and any node that sees a higher number immediately treats older leadership as void.

This is the fencing mechanism for stale leaders. Suppose a partition isolates Kestrel's two `us-east` nodes from the other three. The `us-east` leader, still in term 7, keeps accepting payment writes from clients on its side. The `eu-west` and `ap-south` nodes elect a new leader in term 8. When the partition heals, the old leader receives a message carrying term 8 and steps down. Its term 7 writes never reached a majority, so they never committed, and they are discarded.

Numbering alone does not guarantee safety, because a stale leader can still send messages. What makes it safe is that every acceptance of a message checks the number first. A node rejects anything from a lower term or ballot, so an old leader cannot get a quorum to act on its stale authority.

## 2. Quorum Intersection

Any decision must be acknowledged by a **majority** of nodes. The reason is quorum intersection: any two majorities of a 5-node cluster share at least one node. If a decision was committed by one majority and a later leader needs a majority to decide anything, that later majority must contain a node that remembers the earlier decision.

For Kestrel, the write quorum and the election quorum are both 3. A value committed with acknowledgments from `us-east-1`, `us-east-2`, and `eu-west-1` must be visible to any group of 3 that can win an election, because at least one of those 3 is a node that saw the value. Quorum sizes can be asymmetric in some variants (flexible Paxos, for example), but the invariant remains: every leadership quorum must overlap every commit quorum.

Majorities also determine availability. Kestrel tolerates the loss of any 2 nodes, and it survives the complete loss of either 2-node region, since the remaining 3 nodes still form a quorum. It does not survive losing `ap-south` plus one `us-east` node simultaneously, which leaves only 3 nodes ... actually that case leaves 3 nodes, which is still a majority. The rule to remember is that Kestrel tolerates any 2 node failures, but not 3.

## 3. The Election Restriction

Quorum intersection guarantees that a committed value is known to some node in every future election. It does not guarantee that the node which wins the election knows it. Raft and Zab close that gap with an **election restriction**: a node grants its vote only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own.

In Raft, "up to date" compares the term of the last log entry first, then the log length:

```go
// upToDate reports whether a candidate's log is at least as current as ours
// (Raft §5.4.1). The higher last term wins; on a tie, the longer log wins.
func upToDate(candLastTerm, candLastIndex, myLastTerm, myLastIndex uint64) bool {
	if candLastTerm != myLastTerm {
		return candLastTerm > myLastTerm
	}
	return candLastIndex >= myLastIndex
}
```

Consider Kestrel again. A payment entry at index 42 was acknowledged by `eu-west-1` and `ap-south-1`, forming a commit quorum with the leader. If `us-east-2`, which missed that entry, requests votes, the other nodes refuse because their logs are more current. Only a node holding entry 42 can win, so the committed payment survives leader changes.

Paxos reaches the same guarantee differently. Instead of restricting who may win, it requires the new leader to learn what earlier leaders may have decided, as described next.

## 4. Recovering In-Flight Decisions

A new leader must not invent a value for an index that a previous leader might have already decided. Each protocol handles this with a recovery step.

In **Paxos**, a proposer runs Phase 1: it sends `prepare(n)` to a quorum, and each acceptor replies with the highest-numbered value it has already accepted, if any. If any reply carries a value, the proposer must propose the value with the highest ballot among those replies. Only if no acceptor has accepted anything may the proposer use its own value. This rule is what makes a decision stick even when two proposers collide.

In **Zab**, a newly elected leader runs a discovery phase to find the highest committed transaction among a quorum, then a synchronization phase that brings lagging followers up to that point before any new broadcast begins. Zab's structure, with its explicit phases of discovery, synchronization, and broadcast, makes this recovery visible in the protocol rather than hidden inside the proposal rule.

**Raft** folds recovery into normal operation. A new leader sends heartbeats and log entries, and when a follower's log disagrees with the leader's, the leader walks backward until they match and then overwrites the follower's conflicting suffix. Log Matching ensures that agreement at one index implies agreement on everything before it. The cost is that the leader's log is authoritative, so a follower's uncommitted entries from a dead term may be silently discarded, which is correct but surprising if you have been logging them as "accepted."

## 5. The Commit Rule and Previous-Term Entries

Raft contains a subtle rule that trips up many implementers. A leader must not commit an entry from a previous term merely by counting replicas of it. Instead, it commits only entries from its own current term, and older entries become committed indirectly once a current-term entry on top of them is committed.

The reason is a scenario sometimes called "Figure 8." An entry from term 2 may be stored on a majority of nodes but later overwritten, because a node that never received it can win term 4 and replace it. Committing it by count alone would violate safety. The fix is a check against the current term:

```go
// maybeAdvanceCommit moves commitIndex forward only for entries from the
// current term that a majority of nodes have stored (Raft §5.4.2).
func (n *Node) maybeAdvanceCommit() {
	for idx := n.commitIndex + 1; idx <= n.lastLogIndex(); idx++ {
		if n.log.termAt(idx) != n.currentTerm {
			continue
		}
		if n.countMatchIndex(idx) >= n.quorum() {
			n.commitIndex = idx
		}
	}
}
```

Zab avoids this problem structurally. Its synchronization phase makes a new leader's history the committed prefix before it accepts new transactions, so no previous-epoch entry needs special counting. Paxos avoids it through the Phase 1 value-adoption rule. Each protocol pays for safety in a different place, and when reading any implementation you should locate the place where it does.

## 6. Membership Change

Clusters must grow, shrink, and replace failed hardware. Changing the set of nodes is dangerous because two different majorities can exist at the same moment, one under the old configuration and one under the new, and they might elect different leaders.

Raft offers two solutions. **Joint consensus** runs a transitional configuration in which decisions require a majority of the old set *and* a majority of the new set. **Single-node changes** add or remove one node at a time, which guarantees that the old and new majorities always overlap, at the cost of more steps for large changes. Most production systems use the single-node approach because it is simpler to reason about and to implement correctly.

For Kestrel, replacing the `ap-south-1` node with a node in `ap-south-2` is a single-node change: add the new node first, wait for it to catch up, then remove the old one. Doing it the other way, with only 4 nodes present for a moment, would leave the cluster unable to tolerate any further failure without warning anyone.

Zab handles reconfiguration through its epoch mechanism, and Paxos variants typically use a separate configuration log decided by the same protocol. In every case, the pattern is the same: never let two incompatible majorities coexist without an overlap that forces agreement.

## What to Take Away

These six mechanisms are the vocabulary for reading any consensus implementation. When a system claims to be "Raft-based" or "Paxos-based," ask where it orders leadership attempts, how it guarantees a new leader knows committed history, how it commits old entries, and how it changes membership. The answers reveal most of the safety and failure behavior you will have to operate.

Key takeaway: Consensus protocols are safe because every decision requires an overlapping majority and every new leader must already know the committed history; the mechanisms differ in where they enforce this, and the place they enforce it is where their operational surprises live.

Correction to the previous section: the quorum paragraph in section 2 was muddled. The accurate statement is that Kestrel survives any 2 simultaneous node failures. Losing 3 nodes leaves 2, which is not a majority, so writes stop until a node returns.

# Consensus Trade-offs in Practice

Consensus protocols do not offer free properties. Each design choice buys one guarantee and pays for it somewhere else. Practitioners rarely fail because they picked the "wrong" protocol among Raft, Paxos, and Zab. They fail because they did not notice which trade-off they had accepted. The stories below are illustrative scenarios built on Kestrel's 2/2/1 layout across `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-south`, and each one traces a failure to the mechanism that allowed it.

## 1. Availability Under Partition vs. Write Latency

A majority commit rule means the minority side of a partition cannot make progress. In Kestrel's layout, no single region holds a majority. Every committed write must therefore collect at least one acknowledgment from another region. If the leader sits in `us-east` and the nearest acknowledging node is in `eu-west` at 80 ms round-trip, the write latency floor is roughly that round-trip plus local fsync time. Placing the leader closer to the majority reduces this, but it cannot be eliminated.

**Failure story.** A network fault isolates the two `us-east` nodes from the other three. The `us-east` node that was leader can still accept payment requests, but it cannot reach a quorum, so writes stall. Clients time out after 2 seconds. This is correct behavior: nothing was committed, so nothing is double-charged. The operational problem is that every payment routed through `us-east` fails for the duration of the partition, while the majority side takes several election timeouts to elect a new leader. Customers see errors for an entire region even though the other 3 nodes are healthy.

**Mitigation.** Route clients to the majority side when possible, tune election timeouts against measured cross-region latency, and make every payment request idempotent so that retries after a timeout are safe. Leader placement is a traffic decision as much as a reliability decision.

## 2. Durability vs. Fsync Latency

Raft requires a node to persist `currentTerm`, `votedFor`, and new log entries before it responds to a message. Persisting on every request costs an fsync, which dominates write latency on most hardware. Group commit amortizes this by batching several entries into one fsync, at the price of a small added delay per write.

**Failure story.** To improve benchmark numbers, an engineer disabled fsync on the `ap-south` node's storage and the change was never reverted. The node acknowledges entry 58 and votes for `us-east-2` in term 9. Then power fails. On restart, the node's storage no longer reflects the vote, so it votes for `eu-west-1` in term 9. Both candidates now have 3 votes out of 5:

- `us-east-2` has its own vote, `us-east-1`, and `ap-south-1`.
- `eu-west-1` has its own vote, `eu-west-2`, and `ap-south-1` after restart.

Two leaders exist in one term. Each accepts payments, and the two branches of the ledger diverge. An account may be debited on one branch and not the other. The bug was invisible until reconciliation found mismatched balances several days later.

The fix is to make the vote durable before replying:

```go
// castVote persists the vote before replying to the candidate. If this write
// is lost on a crash, the node may vote twice in one term, and two leaders
// can win the same term.
func (n *Node) castVote(term uint64, candidate string) error {
	if err := n.store.SaveTermAndVote(term, candidate); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	n.sendVoteGranted(candidate, term)
	return nil
}
```

**Mitigation.** Treat fsync as a correctness requirement, not a tuning knob. Verify it with power-loss tests, and alert on any storage configuration that reports write-cache acknowledgments.

## 3. Read Latency vs. Read Consistency

A linearizable read must reflect every write that committed before it started. There are three common ways to serve one, and each trades cost against assumptions:

- **Log reads** route the read through the log. This is always correct and costs a full quorum round trip.
- **ReadIndex** has the leader record its commit index, confirm leadership with one heartbeat round, and then serve from local state. It costs one round trip but no log entry.
- **Leader leases** let the leader serve reads with no round trip, because it trusts that no other leader can exist while its lease is valid. This depends on bounded clock drift between nodes.

**Failure story.** The `us-east` leader holds a lease measured with wall-clock time. Its virtual machine is paused for three seconds by the host during a migration. The `eu-west` nodes elect a new leader, which commits a debit that lowers an account balance. When the paused machine resumes, the old leader still believes its lease is valid and answers a balance query with the pre-debit figure. The customer's authorization check passes, and the account is overdrawn.

**Mitigation.** Use ReadIndex or log reads for any decision that moves money, such as authorization checks. Reserve leases for paths where a bounded staleness is acceptable, such as dashboards, and make the staleness bound an explicit, tested number rather than an assumption.

## 4. Protocol Simplicity vs. Flexibility

Raft was designed to be understandable, and it has many well-tested implementations. Multi-Paxos is flexible, but the foundational Paxos papers describe a single-decree protocol and leave leader management, log compaction, and reconfiguration to the implementer. Zab is tightly coupled to the primary-backup model of its original system, ZooKeeper, which makes it well understood in that context and less portable beyond it.

The trade-off is that a protocol with gaps forces implementers to fill them, and their fills are where bugs live.

**Failure story.** A team building a Multi-Paxos log added a "stable leader" optimization that skips Phase 1 when a new leader takes over, on the assumption that the previous leader is gone. At slot 311, the old leader had already gotten acceptance from two nodes. The new leader proposes its own payment record in slot 311 without learning the earlier accepted value. Different nodes now store different payments for the same slot. No single node reports an error, and the divergence surfaces only when a nightly reconciliation job compares ledgers.

**Mitigation.** Prefer a protocol with a published, widely deployed implementation. If you must extend one, model-check the changes in TLA+ or a similar tool before they reach production, and test leader changes under randomized fault injection.

## 5. Flexible Quorums: Cheap Writes vs. Fragile Elections

Flexible Paxos relaxes the requirement that every quorum be a majority. It requires only that election quorums (Q1) and write quorums (Q2) intersect, which means Q1 + Q2 > N. For Kestrel, a write quorum of 2 and an election quorum of 4 satisfy this. Writes can then commit entirely within `us-east` with no cross-region hop, which lowers latency substantially. The cost is that an election needs 4 nodes, so leadership changes tolerate only one failure.

**Failure story.** Kestrel's writes now commit inside `us-east`. A regional outage takes both `us-east` nodes down at once. Every payment acknowledged in the past several minutes exists only on those two nodes, so those acknowledged payments are lost. This is not an availability problem. It is durability loss, and it occurred because the write quorum was confined to a single failure domain.

**Mitigation.** A write quorum must span the failure domains you need to survive. Flexible quorums are a tool for choosing the latency-durability point deliberately, and the placement of quorum members should be treated as a correctness decision.

## 6. Snapshots and Catch-Up Over the WAN

A node that falls far behind cannot catch up from the log, because the leader has compacted it. It needs a snapshot of the ledger state, which can be large. Transferring that snapshot across regions competes with consensus traffic on the same links.

**Failure story.** The `ap-south` node was offline for six hours and needs a 40 GB snapshot. The transfer saturates the inter-region link, and heartbeats queue behind snapshot chunks. The `eu-west` and `us-east` nodes stop receiving timely heartbeats, start elections, and leadership flaps repeatedly while payments queue behind each change. The catch-up that was meant to restore redundancy temporarily removes availability.

**Mitigation.** Give consensus traffic its own priority class, throttle snapshot transfer, and consider staging snapshots in the lagging node's region ahead of time. Measure catch-up time as part of your recovery plan, not after an incident.

## Summary of Trade-offs

| Decision | Gain | Cost | Failure mode to watch |
|---|---|---|---|
| Majority commit across regions | Survives regional loss | Cross-region write latency | Regional partitions stall writes |
| Fsync on every vote and entry | Election safety | Write latency | Disabled fsync allows double leaders |
| Leases for reads | Low read latency | Trust in clock bounds | Paused leaders serve stale balances |
| Mature protocol implementation | Tested behavior | Less flexibility | Custom shortcuts skip recovery |
| Flexible quorums | Cheaper writes | Failure-domain constraints | Regional loss drops committed data |
| Snapshot catch-up | Restores redundancy | Link contention | Heartbeat starvation causes flapping |

Key takeaway: Every consensus trade-off moves risk rather than eliminating it, so the operational skill is knowing where each choice places its risk: in latency, in clock assumptions, in storage configuration, in quorum placement, or in shared network capacity.

# Consensus in Practice: A Worked Example on Kestrel

This section traces one payment through Kestrel from request to commit, through a leader failure, and into recovery. Then it runs the same scenario through Paxos and Zab. The timings are illustrative, but the sequence of events follows the protocols' rules.

Kestrel's 5 nodes are:

- `us-east-1` (A) and `us-east-2` (B)
- `eu-west-1` (C) and `eu-west-2` (D)
- `ap-south-1` (E)

Round-trip times are about 1 ms within a region, 80 ms between `us-east` and `eu-west`, and 180 ms from `ap-south` to the others. The majority is 3.

## Setup: The State Before the Request

At the start, A is the Raft leader in term 5. The log holds 40 committed entries, and all five nodes have them. Each entry is a ledger operation with a client idempotency key. Entry 40 is a credit to account `acct-7`.

The client wants to debit `acct-7` by 4000 cents with key `pay-9f2`.

## Step 1: A Normal Debit Commits

A receives the request and does three things:

1. It appends entry 41 `{term: 5, key: "pay-9f2", account: "acct-7", amount: -4000}` to its log.
2. It fsyncs the entry before doing anything else.
3. It sends `AppendEntries` to B, C, D, and E in parallel.

B acknowledges in about 1 ms, and C acknowledges at about 80 ms. A now holds three acknowledged copies of entry 41 (A, B, C), which is a majority. A advances its commit index to 41, applies the entry to the ledger, and then responds to the client. D and E have not yet acknowledged, so they will learn the new commit index on the next heartbeat.

The commit rule from earlier applies here. Entry 41 is from the current term, so counting it toward the majority is safe.

## Step 2: The Leader Fails With an Uncommitted Entry

Before its next heartbeat, A appends entry 42 for a different payment and fsyncs it. Only A has entry 42. Then A's host crashes. A has not yet responded to the client for entry 41. Entry 41 is committed, but the client does not know that.

Here is the state after the crash:

| Node | Log through 41 | Entry 42 |
|---|---|---|
| A (crashed) | term 5 | term 5 (only copy) |
| B | term 5 | none |
| C | term 5 | none |
| D | term 5 | none |
| E | term 5 | none |

Entry 41 is on A, B, and C. Entry 42 is on A alone.

## Step 3: Election and Recovery in Raft

D's election timeout fires first. D starts term 6 and requests votes. D's log ends at index 40, which is behind C's and B's, so C refuses. D gets its own vote and E's, which is 2 of 5. It fails, and the term ends without a leader.

B's timeout fires next, and B starts term 7. Its log ends at index 41 in term 5. The up-to-date check works in B's favor:

- C has the same last entry, so C grants its vote.
- D has index 40, so it grants its vote.
- E has index 40, so it grants its vote.

B has 4 votes and becomes leader. It immediately appends a no-op entry at index 42 in term 7 and replicates it. Once the no-op reaches a majority, B commits index 42. That commit also covers entry 41 by the rule from the previous section.

Entry 41 survives because the election restriction ensured that the winner had it. Entry 42 from term 5 is not committed, and no client was told it succeeded, so nothing has to be preserved.

## Step 4: The Client Retries

The client's request for `pay-9f2` timed out, so it retries against B. B has already applied entry 41, and the state machine's idempotency table contains the key:

```go
// applyCommitted applies entries in log order. A duplicate idempotency key
// returns the original result, so client retries after failover are safe.
func (s *Ledger) applyCommitted(entries []Entry) {
	for _, e := range entries {
		if prev, ok := s.results[e.Key]; ok {
			s.reply(e.Index, prev)
			continue
		}
		res := s.debit(e.Account, e.AmountCents)
		s.results[e.Key] = res
		s.reply(e.Index, res)
	}
}
```

The client receives the original result. The account is debited once, not twice. Idempotency at the state machine is what turns an ambiguous timeout into a safe retry.

## Step 5: The Old Leader Rejoins

A restarts as a follower in term 5, with entry 42 still in its log. B sends `AppendEntries` with `prevLogIndex` 41 and term 5. That matches A's entry 41, so the check passes. B's entry 42 in term 7 conflicts with A's entry 42 in term 5, so A truncates its suffix and takes B's entry.

Entry 42 from the old term is gone. It was never committed, and it was never acknowledged, so its disappearance is correct. If the client that submitted it retries, it gets a fresh result.

## The Same Scenario in Paxos

In Multi-Paxos, each log index is a slot decided by its own consensus instance, and a stable leader runs the Phase 1 prepare step only when it changes. Here is how the same events play out:

1. A, as leader in ballot (5, A), gets slot 41 chosen with acceptances from A, B, and C. Slot 42 is accepted by A alone.
2. A crashes. C proposes in ballot (8, C) and sends `prepare` for slots from 41 onward to a quorum.
3. The responses contain the highest-ballot accepted values. Slot 41 appears on several nodes with value "debit pay-9f2," so C must re-propose that exact value. It cannot substitute its own.
4. For slot 42, the result depends on who responded. If A is in the quorum, its accepted value for slot 42 must be re-proposed. If A is not, the leader is free to propose a no-op.

The proposer's rule guarantees that a chosen value stays chosen. The protocol does not need a special entry the way Raft does, but the recovery logic is harder to get right, which is why the trade-off from the previous section applies.

## The Same Scenario in Zab

Zab organizes leadership changes into phases. The events look like this:

1. **Discovery.** A new leader, B, is elected in epoch 6. It collects the last transaction ID (zxid) from a quorum. The highest committed history is zxid (5, 41), which B has.
2. **Synchronization.** B sends C, D, and E the difference they lack. A, when it rejoins, is told to truncate everything after (5, 41), which removes its uncommitted (5, 42).
3. **Broadcast.** B proposes a new transaction at zxid (6, 1), and once a quorum acknowledges it, the transaction commits.

Zab makes the committed prefix explicit before any new broadcast begins, so the commit rule for old entries is not a separate concern.

## What the Walkthrough Shows

Across all three protocols, the same invariants hold:

- A payment is committed only after a majority stores it.
- A new leader must already have, or must learn, every committed entry before it decides anything new.
- An entry that was never committed can be discarded, and the client must be able to retry safely.
- Idempotency keys make the timeout-and-retry path correct.

The differences are in where each protocol enforces these invariants: Raft in the election restriction and log matching, Paxos in the Phase 1 value-adoption rule, and Zab in its discovery and synchronization phases. Knowing where your implementation enforces them tells you where to look when it misbehaves.

Key takeaway: A worked trace shows that consensus safety comes from three things working together, majority commit, a new leader that already holds committed history, and idempotent client retries, and that each protocol enforces that combination at a different step of the leader change.

# Common Consensus Mistakes and How to Catch Them

Most consensus failures in production do not come from misunderstanding the protocol's core. They come from a plausible shortcut that works in every test until a leader changes at the wrong moment, a clock jumps, or a region goes dark. The mistakes below recur across teams using Raft, Paxos, and Zab. For each one, this section describes how it appears in a Kestrel-style payments ledger and how to catch it before customers do.

## 1. Acknowledging Before the Commit Index Advances

A common shortcut is to answer the client as soon as the leader has appended an entry locally, or after it has sent `AppendEntries` to followers, without waiting for a majority. The leader looks fast in benchmarks, but a crash at the wrong moment means the client was told a payment succeeded when it was never committed. A new leader may discard that entry, and the customer's payment disappears.

**How to catch it.** Write a test that crashes the leader at every point between appending an entry and advancing `commitIndex`, then checks that any acknowledged payment survives. Fault injection tools such as Jepsen-style harnesses, or deterministic simulators that control message delivery and crash points, are well suited to this. The invariant to assert is simple: every acknowledged payment must appear in the final ledger on every node that has committed it.

## 2. Counting Old-Term Entries Toward a Commit

This is the Figure 8 mistake from earlier. A leader sees an entry from an earlier term stored on a majority and commits it immediately. The entry can later be overwritten by a leader that never saw it. Code that looks obviously correct passes almost every test, because the bad sequence requires specific leader churn.

**How to catch it.** Script the exact sequence on a 5-node model of Kestrel: a term-2 entry reaches three nodes, the leader crashes, a node without that entry wins a later term, and the old entry is overwritten. Then run randomized leader churn at scale. A simulator that varies message order and crash timing will find this faster than hand-written tests. Model checking the commit rule in TLA+ is also effective, because the counterexample it produces is the exact sequence.

## 3. Trusting Wall-Clock Time for Leases

Leader leases let a leader serve reads without a quorum round trip, but they assume the leader and other nodes agree on elapsed time within a bound. Teams often implement leases with wall-clock timestamps, which NTP corrections can step backward or forward. A paused virtual machine resumes believing its lease is still valid. The stale-balance failure in the trade-offs section is the typical outcome.

**How to catch it.** Inject clock faults: step the clock, slow it, and pause the process for longer than the lease duration. Then issue reads during the paused window and check them against the committed history. Use a linearizability checker, such as Porcupine or Elle, on the recorded operation history. A lease that is safe only when clocks behave is not safe. Make the drift bound an explicit configuration value, and alert when measured drift approaches it.

## 4. Skipping Paxos Phase 1 for "Stable" Leaders

Multi-Paxos implementations often skip the prepare phase when a leader is believed stable, as an optimization. The belief is usually wrong during failover. The earlier example showed a payment record at slot 311 overwritten because the new leader proposed its own value without learning the accepted one.

**How to catch it.** Run concurrent proposers in a deterministic simulator and assert agreement: no two nodes may record different values for the same slot. Model the optimization explicitly in TLA+ and check agreement under a failover. The bug also shows up in a reconciliation job that compares ledgers across nodes. Treat any mismatch as a safety incident, not a data-cleanup task.

## 5. Unsafe Membership Changes

Adding two nodes at once, or switching configurations without joint consensus or single-node steps, can create two disjoint majorities. Kestrel's cluster of 5 going to 7 by adding `eu-west-3` and `us-east-3` in one step is an example. Each configuration may elect its own leader, and both leaders can commit.

**How to catch it.** Make every membership change go through a reviewed procedure and test it under partitions. Check that old and new majorities always overlap at every intermediate configuration. A simple invariant check is useful in code review and in tests. The placement validator below covers the region-level version of this problem.

## 6. Non-Idempotent Client Retries

Consensus guarantees that a committed entry is not lost. It does not guarantee the client knows whether its request committed. A timeout is ambiguous. Without idempotency keys, a retry after a leader change debits the account twice. Teams often assume the consensus layer provides exactly-once semantics, and it does not.

**How to catch it.** Inject request timeouts that occur after the commit but before the response, and assert the ledger balance after retries matches the number of distinct payment keys. Run this check continuously in a staging environment with synthetic traffic and compare totals against an independent record. A duplicate-charge counter that is not zero is a bug.

## 7. Stale Reads From Followers

Serving reads from a follower's local state without confirming leadership or waiting for the commit index returns old data. A balance check served from a lagging follower can authorize a payment that the cluster has already spent. This is a more subtle version of the lease problem and is often introduced for read scaling.

**How to catch it.** Record client-visible operation histories, including invocation and response times, and check them with a linearizability checker. Any read that returns a value older than a write that completed before the read began is a violation. Route payment-authorization reads through ReadIndex or a log read, and reserve follower reads for paths that explicitly accept bounded staleness.

## 8. Timeouts That Cause Constant Elections

Election timeouts that are too short relative to the network, or that are not randomized, cause split votes and repeated leadership changes. Each change pauses writes. A node that rejoins after a brief partition can also disrupt a stable leader by starting an election with a higher term, unless the protocol uses a pre-vote phase.

**How to catch it.** Measure leadership changes per hour and write latency during each change, and alert on the change rate rather than on individual elections. Test with an asymmetric partition in which one link flaps. The fix is usually to set timeouts as a multiple of measured cross-region round-trip time, randomize them, and enable pre-vote where the library supports it.

## 9. Placing Quorum Members in One Failure Domain

This is the most expensive mistake in practice, because it looks like a sensible deployment. A team places 3 of Kestrel's 5 nodes in `us-east`, perhaps because that region has the most capacity. A regional outage then removes the majority in one event. The cluster stops accepting payments, and if writes were confined to that region, committed data may be lost.

**How to catch it.** Validate placement before deployment. The following check fails if any region holds a majority or if the node count is even, which adds no fault tolerance:

```go
package topology

import "fmt"

type NodeInfo struct {
	ID     string
	Region string
}

// validatePlacement rejects layouts where losing one region breaks quorum,
// and rejects even node counts, which add no fault tolerance over one fewer.
func validatePlacement(nodes []NodeInfo) error {
	if len(nodes)%2 == 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf("even node count %d adds no fault tolerance", len(nodes))
	}
	quorum := len(nodes)/2 + 1
	perRegion := make(map[string]int)
	for _, n := range nodes {
		perRegion[n.Region]++
	}
	for region, count := range perRegion {
		if count >= quorum {
			return fmt.Errorf("region %s holds %d of %d nodes: its loss breaks quorum",
				region, count, len(nodes))
		}
	}
	return nil
}
```

Kestrel's 2/2/1 layout passes this check, because no region holds the quorum of 3. Run the check in CI against the deployment manifest, and rehearse a full regional failure on a schedule. A layout that has never been tested against a region loss has not been tested.

## 10. Snapshot and Catch-Up Neglect

Teams often leave log compaction and snapshot transfer untested until a lagging node needs one. A large snapshot over a WAN link can starve heartbeats and cause the flapping described in the trade-offs section. Compaction that never runs lets the log grow until restarts take minutes.

**How to catch it.** Track log length, snapshot install duration, and heartbeat jitter during catch-up. Practice recovery of a node that has been offline for a long period, and measure how long it takes to return to quorum membership. Treat catch-up time as a service-level objective, not a curiosity.

## 11. Misunderstanding Ambiguous Failures in Operations

Operators often read a leader change or a timeout in the logs as a failed write. Runbooks that instruct staff to "re-run" a payment after an error can cause duplicate charges, because the original may have committed. The protocol's behavior is correct; the operational assumption is the mistake.

**How to catch it.** Make the runbook reference idempotency keys, and require lookup of the key's recorded result before any manual retry. Audit a sample of manual interventions against the ledger each week.

## A Checklist for Reviews

When reviewing a consensus-based design or change, ask these questions:

- Does the client receive a success response only after the commit index covers the entry?
- Does the commit rule refuse to count old-term entries on their own?
- Does every read that affects money go through a path that is linearizable under clock faults?
- Are the election timeouts randomized and tied to measured latency?
- Is every membership change overlapping at every step?
- Are retries protected by idempotency keys at the state machine?
- Does the placement survive the loss of any single failure domain?

Each question corresponds to a test or a metric. If a design cannot answer one of them with evidence, that gap is the place to start.

Key takeaway: The most damaging consensus mistakes are shortcuts that hold under normal operation and break only during leader changes, clock faults, or regional loss, so the way to catch them is deliberate fault injection, linearizability checking, and placement validation rather than code review alone.

# Consensus and Its Alternatives

Raft, Paxos, and Zab all solve the same problem: agreeing on one ordered sequence of decisions across nodes that can crash and messages that can be lost or delayed. Other designs make different trade-offs. Some give up ordering, some give up agreement, and some assume nodes can lie. Choosing well requires knowing what each alternative guarantees and what it leaves to the application.

This section compares the three consensus protocols with the approaches most often considered in their place: leaderless quorum systems, asynchronous primary-backup, two-phase commit, Byzantine fault tolerant protocols, and sharded consensus. Kestrel, our payments ledger on 5 nodes across `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-south`, anchors each comparison.

## Leaderless Quorum Systems

Dynamo-style systems, including Cassandra and Riak, have no leader. A client writes to several nodes and reads from several nodes, and the system is correct when the read and write quorums overlap (R + W > N). Conflicts are handled by version vectors, last-writer-wins timestamps, or merge functions such as CRDTs.

The core difference is ordering. A leaderless system does not agree on a single sequence of operations, so two concurrent writes may both succeed and be reconciled afterward. That is acceptable for a shopping cart and dangerous for money.

Consider a Kestrel account with a balance of 100. Two debits of 80 arrive at different coordinators within the same few milliseconds. Each coordinator reads a quorum, sees 100, and writes a balance of 20 to its quorum. Both writes succeed. The system now holds two conflicting balances that reconciliation cannot merge into a correct answer, because the correct answer is to reject one debit, and reconciliation cannot make that decision without reversing a payment the customer already saw succeed.

Consensus avoids this by making the balance check and the debit one step in a single order:

```go
// Under consensus, every debit is checked against the balance produced by
// all earlier committed entries, so the second debit above is rejected.
func (l *Ledger) applyDebit(e Entry) error {
	if l.balances[e.Account]+e.AmountCents < 0 {
		return ErrInsufficientFunds
	}
	l.balances[e.Account] += e.AmountCents
	return nil
}
```

Leaderless systems excel where operations commute, where availability during partitions matters more than strict invariants, and where write throughput must scale across many keys. They are a poor fit for invariants that depend on ordering, such as non-negative balances or uniqueness of a payment identifier.

## Asynchronous Primary-Backup

A primary accepts writes, returns success, and ships the change to standby nodes in the background. Failover promotes a standby. This design has the lowest write latency of any option, because the client does not wait for remote acknowledgment.

Its failure mode is precise. If the primary fails after acknowledging a payment but before the standby received it, the promoted standby does not have the payment. The customer saw success, and the ledger does not record it. Some systems mitigate this with semi-synchronous shipping, where the primary waits for one standby, but that is not a guarantee. A single standby that is unreachable makes the system choose between blocking writes and risking loss, and failover logic without a consensus decision cannot reliably tell which case it is in.

Consensus-based designs pay the round-trip cost up front to close this gap. For Kestrel, a write committed with acknowledgments from `us-east-2`, `eu-west-1`, and `ap-south-1` cannot disappear through a leader change, because any election quorum overlaps it. Asynchronous primary-backup is appropriate for data that can be rebuilt from another source, such as caches, search indexes, and analytics.

## Two-Phase Commit

Two-phase commit (2PC) is an atomic commitment protocol, not a consensus protocol in the strict sense. A coordinator asks participants to prepare, then tells them to commit or abort once all have voted. It guarantees that a transaction spanning several shards either applies everywhere or nowhere.

Its well-known weakness is blocking. If the coordinator fails after participants have prepared, they must wait for its decision and cannot release locks unilaterally. Three-phase commit reduces blocking under some assumptions but is not safe under partitions.

The practical solution is to make the coordinator and participants themselves consensus groups. Spanner does this, running Paxos within each shard and 2PC across shards. For Kestrel, a transfer between `acct-7` in one shard and `acct-912` in another is a 2PC transaction whose participants are each a 5-node consensus group. A coordinator crash no longer blocks the transfer indefinitely, because the coordinator's decision is itself recorded through consensus and can be recovered.

2PC is the right tool when a single operation must touch several independent ledgers. It is never a substitute for consensus within one ledger.

## Byzantine Fault Tolerant Protocols

Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) and its successors, including HotStuff, tolerate nodes that behave arbitrarily, including lying and sending conflicting messages. A cluster tolerating f Byzantine nodes needs at least 3f + 1 nodes, and its quorums are larger than in crash-fault protocols.

For Kestrel, f = 1 requires at least 4 nodes, so the 5-node layout could tolerate one malicious node. The costs are substantial. Messages are signed and verified, communication in PBFT is quadratic in the number of nodes, and HotStuff reduces that to linear at the cost of more protocol phases. Throughput is typically lower than a crash-fault protocol on the same hardware.

Byzantine protocols are justified when nodes belong to different operators who do not trust each other, such as in a multi-party settlement network. Kestrel's 5 nodes are operated by one team under one trust boundary, so the crash-fault assumption that Raft, Paxos, and Zab make is the correct one. Using a Byzantine protocol here would impose real cost for a threat the system does not face. Hardware and software integrity controls, such as signed binaries and attestation, address the corruption cases that matter in a single operator's environment.

## Sharded Consensus

A single consensus group has a throughput ceiling set by its leader, so large systems partition their data into many groups. Each group runs its own consensus, and cross-group operations use 2PC or a similar protocol. Multi-Raft implementations and Spanner's Paxos groups follow this pattern.

For Kestrel, partitioning accounts across several 5-node groups multiplies throughput, because each group has its own leader and log. The cost is operational: 5 groups means 25 nodes, placement must be checked per group, leadership must be balanced across regions, and every cross-account transfer becomes a distributed transaction. Sharding is the right response to a throughput limit that has been measured, not a default.

## Comparison

| Approach | Ordering | Failure assumption | Write latency | Failover loss risk | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Raft, Paxos, Zab | Total order per group | Crash-fault | One cross-region quorum round trip | None for committed data | Ledgers, locks, metadata |
| Leaderless quorum | None (merge later) | Crash-fault | Lowest available quorum | Concurrent conflicts | Commutative data, high availability |
| Async primary-backup | Single writer | Crash-fault | Local only | Acknowledged data can be lost | Rebuildable data |
| 2PC over consensus groups | Atomic across groups | Crash-fault | Two rounds per group | None when groups are consensus-backed | Cross-shard transactions |
| PBFT / HotStuff | Total order per group | Byzantine | Higher than crash-fault | None for committed data | Mutually distrusting operators |
| Sharded consensus | Total order per shard | Crash-fault | As per group | None within a shard | Throughput beyond one group |

Among the three protocols under discussion, Raft, Paxos, and Zab differ mainly in how they structure leadership and recovery, not in what they guarantee. Viewstamped Replication, the older design that Raft closely resembles, provides the same guarantees with a different view-change structure. Choosing among them is usually a question of available implementations and team familiarity rather than a difference in safety.

## Choosing for Kestrel

Kestrel needs total order and non-negative balances, which rules out leaderless designs and asynchronous primary-backup for the ledger itself. It operates under one trust boundary, which rules out Byzantine protocols. It is a single ledger at current volume, which means one consensus group is sufficient, with sharding held in reserve. Cross-account transfers that span shards will eventually need 2PC over consensus groups, and that is a later design decision.

Within consensus, the choice of Raft, Paxos, or Zab should follow the maturity of the implementation the team will operate, the ability to test it under fault injection, and the operators' familiarity with its failure modes.

Key takeaway: Consensus is the right foundation for an ordered, invariant-bearing ledger, and each alternative trades away ordering, failure assumptions, or latency in ways that suit other workloads, so the design decision is to match the guarantee to the invariant rather than to the most scalable option.

# Frequently Asked Questions About Consensus Algorithms

These questions come up repeatedly when teams first adopt Raft, Paxos, or Zab, or when they review a design that uses one. The answers refer back to Kestrel, our payments ledger on 5 nodes across `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-south`, and to the mechanisms covered in earlier sections.

## 1. Do I need consensus, or is a transactional database enough?

Often a transactional database is enough, and it is the better choice. Most production databases, including managed offerings, already run a consensus protocol internally to order their writes across the machines they manage. If your Kestrel ledger stores its data in such a database and you rely on its transactions and its replication settings, you are already depending on consensus, and you did not have to implement it.

You need to run consensus yourself in a narrower set of cases. The first is when you are building the coordination layer itself, such as a lock service, a configuration store, or the metadata store for a sharded system. The second is when you need a specific ordering guarantee that a database does not expose, for example a sequence of state transitions in your own state machine. The third is when a managed service's failover behavior or write latency does not meet your requirements and you have the operational capacity to own those trade-offs.

The practical test is whether you can name the invariant you need and show that no existing component enforces it. "Ledger balances never go negative and no payment applies twice" is an invariant, and a transactional database with appropriate constraints usually enforces it. "Exactly one of these five nodes may hold the right to sign settlement files at a time" is a coordination invariant, and it is a candidate for a consensus-backed lease. Building consensus when a database would do adds operational risk without adding safety.

## 2. Why does a cluster need a majority, and why is Kestrel 5 nodes rather than 4?

A majority is the smallest group that guarantees any two groups share at least one node. That shared node is how a decision made in one leadership attempt becomes visible to the next. Without the overlap, a new leader could be elected without knowing about a committed payment, and the protocol's safety would fail.

The fault tolerance of a cluster of size n is the number of nodes it can lose while keeping a majority:

```go
// faultTolerance returns how many nodes a cluster of size n can lose
// and still form a majority.
func faultTolerance(n int) int {
	return (n - 1) / 2
}
```

For Kestrel, `faultTolerance(5)` is 2, and `faultTolerance(4)` is 1. A 4-node cluster tolerates only one failure, which is the same as a 3-node cluster, but it costs more and needs a larger majority for every write. That is why clusters are sized with odd numbers. Kestrel uses 5 rather than 3 because it must survive the loss of a region with 2 nodes and still keep a majority, which 3 nodes cannot do across three regions.

The majority requirement also means that losing too many nodes stops writes entirely. If Kestrel loses 3 nodes, the remaining 2 cannot form a majority, and payments stop until a node returns. This is the intended behavior. The system chooses unavailability over the risk of two leaders accepting conflicting debits.

## 3. Can a leader be wrong, and what happens to writes it has already accepted?

A leader can be wrong in the sense that it may have been deposed without knowing it. A leader that is partitioned from the majority keeps believing it is in charge until it hears a higher term or ballot. During that window it may accept entries, but it cannot commit them, because it cannot reach a majority.

Those uncommitted entries are discarded when the partition heals and the old leader learns about the new leadership. Its log is truncated to match the new leader's, as in the Raft walkthrough. The entry was never committed, so no node is required to keep it.

The important distinction is between accepted and committed. An entry is committed once a majority stores it, and only committed entries are guaranteed to survive. A client that receives a success response after commit has a guarantee. A client that receives a timeout does not know whether its write committed, and it must retry safely. For Kestrel, that is why every debit carries an idempotency key. If the original debit committed before the leader changed, the retry returns the original result. If it did not commit, the retry applies it once. Consensus does not decide what the client sees after an ambiguous failure, and the application must be built to handle that case.

## 4. Which protocol should I choose: Raft, Paxos, or Zab?

For a new system, choose Raft unless you have a specific reason not to. It separates leader election, log replication, and membership change into clearly named parts, and it has many mature implementations in several languages, including a widely used Go library from etcd. Teams can read the protocol, reason about its states, and test those states directly. That understandability matters because most consensus incidents come from misunderstood recovery paths.

Zab is the right choice when you are building on ZooKeeper or running a system designed around its primary-backup model. Its discovery and synchronization phases are well defined, and its operational tooling is tied to ZooKeeper. Choosing Zab for a new system without a ZooKeeper dependency gives you a less common implementation and a protocol whose guarantees are harder to test in isolation.

Paxos is the right choice in two situations. The first is when you already operate a Paxos-based system and want to extend it. The second is when you need the flexibility of its design, such as flexible quorums, and you have the expertise to implement the parts the original papers leave open. Multi-Paxos implementations differ widely in their leader handling and recovery, so the protocol's name tells you little about its behavior. Read the specific implementation's recovery path before trusting it.

Whichever you choose, the safety depends on the implementation. A correct Raft implementation and a buggy one share a name but not a guarantee. Test the one you deploy.

## 5. How do I know my consensus deployment is actually safe?

No amount of reading the protocol proves a deployment is safe. Safety is established by testing the deployed system under the faults it will face, and by checking its external behavior against a correctness specification.

Start with fault injection that covers the cases where bugs hide: leader crashes at every step of commit, network partitions that isolate a leader, clock steps and process pauses, and disk failures that lose unfsynced data. Record the client-visible history of operations, including when each request was sent and when its response arrived. Then run a linearizability checker such as Porcupine or Elle against that history. A checker finds the cases where a read returned data older than a write that had already completed, which is the symptom most stale-read bugs produce.

Add configuration checks that run before deployment. The placement validator in the mistakes section catches layouts where one failure domain holds a majority, and it catches even node counts. Run it in CI against the deployment manifest, and fail the build when it fails.

Finally, measure continuously in production. Track leadership changes per hour, write latency during each change, time to catch up a lagging node, and any mismatch between ledger totals and an independent record. Each of these signals corresponds to a failure mode described earlier. A change in any of them is a reason to investigate before the next incident does.

A consensus deployment that has been tested under these conditions is not guaranteed to be correct, but it has been checked against the failures that actually happen. That is the most any team can honestly claim.

Key takeaway: Consensus is worth its cost only where you need an ordered, invariant-bearing decision and no existing component provides it, the majority rule is what makes both availability and safety predictable, and every claim about a deployment's safety has to rest on tests under fault injection rather than on the protocol's name.

# Executive Summary: Consensus Algorithms for Engineering Leadership

## What Consensus Is

Consensus is how a group of nodes agrees on one ordered sequence of decisions when some nodes fail and messages can be lost or delayed. Raft, Paxos, and Zab are three protocols that provide this guarantee. They differ in how they are structured and implemented, not in what they guarantee. Each one ensures that a committed decision survives failures and that all nodes see decisions in the same order.

For our payments ledger, Kestrel, this means a payment that the system confirmed to a customer will not disappear during a server failure or a regional outage, and two conflicting debits against the same balance cannot both succeed.

## Why It Matters to the Business

Kestrel runs on 5 nodes across three regions: 2 in `us-east`, 2 in `eu-west`, and 1 in `ap-south`. This layout means:

- **Any 2 nodes can fail** without stopping payments or losing confirmed transactions.
- **The loss of an entire region** with 2 nodes does not stop the system, because the remaining 3 nodes still form a majority.
- **The cost is latency.** Every confirmed payment waits for acknowledgment from a node in another region. Typical added delay is on the order of the cross-region round trip, tens of milliseconds for `us-east` to `eu-west`.

The trade-off leadership is accepting is this: slightly slower writes and more operational complexity in exchange for protection against lost or double-applied payments. For a payments system, that is almost always the correct trade. Losing one confirmed payment costs more in reconciliation, customer support, and regulatory exposure than the latency is worth.

## What Consensus Does Not Solve

Consensus is not a complete correctness solution. Three things remain the application's responsibility:

- **Client retries.** When a request times out, the client cannot know whether it committed. Every payment must carry an idempotency key so retries are safe. This is a product and API requirement, not a protocol feature.
- **Availability under majority loss.** If 3 of Kestrel's 5 nodes are lost, payments stop until one returns. This is deliberate: the system chooses to stop rather than risk conflicting records. Leadership should decide whether that behavior matches customer commitments.
- **Operational discipline.** Protocols are correct only when deployed and operated correctly. Most serious incidents in consensus systems come from misconfigured storage, unsafe shortcuts, or placement that concentrates nodes in one failure domain, not from the protocol itself.

## Choosing Among the Options

| Option | Use when | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| Managed or transactional database | The invariant is expressible as a database constraint | Vendor failover behavior must meet your requirements |
| Raft (recommended default) | You build or operate a coordination layer | Requires in-house expertise to operate well |
| Zab | You are building on ZooKeeper | Narrower ecosystem outside that stack |
| Paxos | You already run a Paxos system | Implementations differ widely in recovery behavior |
| Leaderless or asynchronous replication | Data is rebuildable or conflicts are acceptable | Confirmed writes can be lost or conflict |

For Kestrel, the recommended path is a consensus-backed store for the ledger, using a mature implementation rather than a custom one. Build a consensus layer in-house only if the business needs a coordination service that no existing product provides.

## Recommendations

1. **Confirm the invariant.** For each system proposed for consensus, name the invariant it must protect. If a database constraint or an existing managed service enforces it, prefer that.
2. **Fund testing before features.** Budget for fault-injection testing, linearizability checking, and regional failure exercises. Teams that skip this usually discover their failure behavior during an incident.
3. **Review placement as a risk decision.** No single region should hold a majority of any consensus group. Require an automated check in the deployment pipeline.
4. **Require idempotency end to end.** Make it a standard for every API that moves money.
5. **Set measurable service levels.** Track write latency, leadership changes per hour, time to catch up a recovering node, and any mismatch between the ledger and independent records. Review these monthly.
6. **Plan for growth.** A single consensus group has a throughput ceiling. Reserve the design decision about sharding and cross-shard transactions for when measured load requires it.

## Decisions Needed From Leadership

- Accept the latency cost of cross-region commits for the payments ledger, or direct engineering to evaluate a regional layout with different trade-offs.
- Approve the investment in fault-injection testing and a recurring regional failover exercise.
- Confirm the availability posture during majority loss: payments pause rather than risk inconsistency.
- Decide whether the organization will operate its own consensus layer or rely on a managed service for the ledger.

## Bottom Line

Consensus is the established, well-understood way to keep a payments ledger correct through failures. Its costs are real and predictable: higher write latency and more operational rigor. The main risks are not in the protocols themselves but in how they are deployed, tested, and used by client applications. Leadership's most effective levers are funding testing, insisting on idempotent APIs, and requiring a placement review before any change goes to production.

Key takeaway: Consensus is the right foundation for Kestrel's ledger because it trades a modest, predictable increase in write latency for protection against lost or double-applied payments, and the business return depends on funding the testing, idempotency, and placement discipline that make that protection real in production.

# Closing: What Consensus Gives Us and What It Does Not

Consensus lets a group of nodes agree on one ordered sequence of decisions despite crashes, lost messages, and partitions. Across this part of the guide, we have examined Raft, Paxos, and Zab through the same lens: what each guarantees, how it recovers from a leader change, and where it fails in practice.

## What We Covered

The section opened with six mechanisms that appear in every consensus protocol: term or ballot numbering, quorum intersection, the election restriction, recovery of in-flight decisions, the commit rule for entries from earlier terms, and membership change. These are the vocabulary for reading any implementation.

We then looked at trade-offs. Majority commit buys survival of regional loss at the cost of cross-region write latency. Durable storage of votes and entries buys election safety at the cost of fsync latency. Leases buy fast reads at the cost of trusting clock bounds. Flexible quorums buy cheaper writes at the cost of narrower failure tolerance, and each choice has a concrete failure story on Kestrel's 2/2/1 layout.

The worked example traced one payment through a normal commit, a leader failure with an uncommitted entry, election, client retry, and the old leader's rejoin. The code sketch showed the vote check, the log-matching check, the current-term commit rule, Paxos value adoption, and Zab discovery in roughly 200 lines of Go. We compared consensus with leaderless quorums, asynchronous primary-backup, two-phase commit, Byzantine protocols, and sharding, and we saw that the right choice depends on the invariant being protected.

## What Consensus Does Not Do

Consensus does not make a system correct on its own. Three limits recur throughout the material:

- **It orders decisions within one group.** It says nothing about operations that span several groups. A transfer from one shard to another is not made atomic by consensus inside either shard.
- **It cannot resolve ambiguity for clients.** A timeout does not reveal whether a write committed. Idempotency keys at the state machine remain the application's responsibility.
- **It is only as safe as its deployment.** Storage that acknowledges unflushed writes, clocks that jump, and placement that concentrates a majority in one failure domain all break guarantees the protocol provides on paper.

## A Consolidated Checklist

Before a consensus-backed system goes to production, confirm:

1. Clients receive success only after commit, and retries are idempotent.
2. Votes and log entries are fsynced before any reply that depends on them.
3. The commit rule refuses to count old-term entries on their own.
4. Reads that affect money use ReadIndex or log reads, not follower state or unchecked leases.
5. Election timeouts are randomized and tied to measured latency.
6. Membership changes overlap at every intermediate step.
7. Placement passes the region-loss check, and an odd node count is in use.
8. Fault injection and linearizability checking run in CI and on a schedule.

## Looking Ahead: Transactions

Kestrel now has a correct foundation for a single ledger. The next gap appears as soon as a business operation touches more than one ledger. Suppose the accounts for a transfer live in different shards, each a separate consensus group. A naive implementation performs two independent writes:

```go
// transferNaive performs two independent writes with no shared decision.
// If the process crashes between them, the debit is committed and the
// credit never happens, and no component will notice the gap.
func transferNaive(from, to *Shard, acct, dest string, cents int64) error {
	if err := from.Debit(acct, cents); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return to.Credit(dest, cents)
}
```

Consensus inside each shard makes each write durable and ordered. It does not make the pair of writes atomic. The next section, on transactions, addresses that problem. It covers atomic commitment across partitions, why two-phase commit works and where it blocks, how a coordinator's decision can itself be made durable through consensus, and what isolation guarantees Kestrel can offer clients when transfers overlap in time. Those questions determine whether a transfer is all-or-nothing, and they determine what a customer can observe while one is in progress.

Key takeaway: Consensus gives Kestrel a durable, totally ordered history for each ledger, but a transfer that spans ledgers still needs an atomic commitment protocol, and the next section examines how to build one without reintroducing the blocking and ambiguity that consensus was used to remove.

# CAP and Consistency Models: An Overview

Every distributed data system makes a promise about what a reader will see after a write. The CAP theorem and the consistency model hierarchy describe the range of promises a system can make and the costs of each. Engineers who understand this range can say precisely what a system guarantees, instead of relying on labels like "strongly consistent" or "highly available" that mean different things to different teams.

This section gives the overview. It defines the theorem precisely, corrects the most common misreadings, lays out the consistency models that matter in practice, and maps them onto Kestrel, our payments ledger running on 5 nodes across `us-east`, `eu-west`, and `ap-south`.

## What the CAP Theorem Actually Says

Eric Brewer proposed the conjecture in 2000, and Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a version of it in 2002. The formal statement is narrow. In an asynchronous network model, where messages may be delayed arbitrarily and nodes may fail, no data system can simultaneously provide:

- **Consistency**, meaning linearizability: every operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its invocation and its response, and the order of those points is consistent with real time.
- **Availability**, meaning every request received by a non-failing node receives a response.
- **Partition tolerance**, meaning the system keeps operating when messages between nodes are lost.

The theorem says that when a partition occurs, a system must give up either consistency or availability for at least some requests. It does not say the system must choose between them permanently, and it does not say that partitions are optional.

The "pick two of three" phrasing is widely repeated and misleading. Partitions are not a feature a system can opt out of, because any network can partition. The real choice is what a system does during a partition, and that choice can be made per operation.

## Three Common Misreadings

**The C in CAP is not ACID consistency.** ACID consistency concerns application invariants, such as a balance never going negative. CAP's consistency is linearizability, a property about the order and visibility of individual operations. A system can be ACID-consistent for transactions and still fail CAP's consistency for single-key reads.

**Availability is about every request, not average uptime.** If a minority of nodes is cut off and refuses to answer, the system is not available by CAP's definition, even if 99.99 percent of traffic succeeds. The theorem is about the response to each request, not the aggregate.

**CAP says nothing about latency.** The PACELC extension states the missing half: during a partition, choose availability or consistency; otherwise, choose latency or consistency. Most design trade-offs in practice happen in the "else" branch. Kestrel's cross-region commits pay latency for consistency even when no partition exists.

## Kestrel During a Partition

Suppose the two `us-east` nodes are cut off from the other three. Kestrel's options are concrete:

- **Consistency preference (CP).** The majority side of 3 nodes keeps accepting payments, which are linearizable because they go through the consensus log. The minority side refuses writes and returns an error. Customers in `us-east` see failed payments for the duration of the partition, but no balance is ever inconsistent.
- **Availability preference (AP).** Both sides accept writes. The two sides diverge, and when the partition heals, conflicting debits must be reconciled. For a payments ledger, reconciliation can only reject or reverse a debit the customer already saw succeed, which is not an acceptable outcome.

Kestrel is a CP system for writes. The question for the rest of this section is what can be relaxed safely, and for which operations.

## The Consistency Model Hierarchy

Consistency models are ordered from strongest to weakest, with stronger models constraining the system more and costing more to provide.

**Strict serializability** combines serializable transactions with real-time ordering. Transactions appear to execute one at a time in an order consistent with their actual start and end times. This is the strongest model practical systems provide for multi-key work, and it is what Kestrel needs for transfers that span accounts.

**Linearizability** applies the same real-time requirement to single-object operations. Once a payment is confirmed, every subsequent read anywhere in the system reflects it. Kestrel's balance checks for authorization must be linearizable, which is why they use ReadIndex or log reads, as covered in the trade-offs section.

**Sequential consistency** keeps every node's view of operations in some single order, but that order need not match real time. A node may observe a write later than another node, as long as all nodes agree on the sequence. It is weaker than linearizability and rarely offered alone.

**Causal consistency** preserves cause and effect. If one operation could have influenced another, every node sees them in that order. Operations with no causal relationship may be seen in different orders by different nodes. For Kestrel, a refund that references a payment must never appear before the payment, but two unrelated payments on different accounts may appear in either order.

**Session guarantees** constrain what a single client sees across its own requests. Read-your-writes ensures a client sees its own confirmed payments. Monotonic reads ensures a client never sees a balance move backward. These guarantees are cheap to provide and often sufficient for user-facing views.

**Eventual consistency** guarantees only that, if writes stop, all nodes eventually converge to the same value. It says nothing about what is read in the meantime, and it does not prevent lost updates unless the system adds conflict resolution.

Consider a session guarantee in code. A client carries the highest commit index it has observed, and a reader serves only if it has applied at least that far. This is the mechanism behind read-your-writes on a follower:

```go
// Reader serves reads from locally applied state. It is a follower-side view
// of the ledger, not the consensus log itself.
type Reader struct {
	mu       sync.Mutex
	applied  uint64
	balances map[string]int64
}

// readAtLeast serves a read only if this reader has applied at least the
// session's last-observed commit index. Otherwise the caller must retry or
// route to a node that has caught up.
func (r *Reader) readAtLeast(minIndex uint64, account string) (int64, error) {
	r.mu.Lock()
	defer r.mu.Unlock()

	if r.applied < minIndex {
		return 0, ErrStale
	}
	return r.balances[account], nil
}
```

The session carries `minIndex`, which is cheap to pass with each response. The reader never returns state older than what the client has already seen, so a customer who saw a payment confirmed will not see the old balance on the next screen, even when that read is served locally.

## Mapping Operations to Models

The useful question is not which model the system has, but which model each operation requires. For Kestrel:

| Operation | Required model | How Kestrel provides it |
|---|---|---|
| Authorize a payment against balance | Linearizable | ReadIndex or log read on the leader |
| Apply a debit | Linearizable, idempotent | Consensus log with idempotency key |
| Transfer across two accounts | Strict serializable | Atomic commitment across shards (next section) |
| Show a customer their recent payments | Read-your-writes, monotonic reads | Session token with minimum applied index |
| Compute daily analytics totals | Eventual, bounded staleness | Asynchronous copies to an analytics store |

The pattern is that money movement needs linearizability, customer-facing views need session guarantees, and analytics can tolerate staleness. Paying for the strongest model everywhere is expensive and unnecessary. Paying for the weakest model everywhere is dangerous.

## Common Errors

Teams usually make three mistakes with consistency. They label a system "strongly consistent" without naming the model, which hides whether single-key reads, transactions, or cross-region reads are covered. They route money-moving reads to followers for latency and then discover that authorization decisions were based on stale balances. They use last-writer-wins timestamps to resolve conflicts, which loses updates whenever clocks disagree and which is never acceptable for a ledger.

A precise statement of the model for each operation prevents all three. It also gives the test suite a target: a linearizability checker can verify a linearizable claim, and a session test can verify read-your-writes.

## What Comes Next

This overview frames the rest of the section. The next topics take each model in turn, starting with the mechanisms for linearizable reads, then session guarantees, causal ordering, and conflict resolution in leaderless systems. Each one will be evaluated against Kestrel's operations, with the cost of each guarantee measured in latency and in operational complexity.

Key takeaway: CAP forces a choice only during partitions, and consistency models let a system choose the weakest guarantee each operation can safely accept, so Kestrel should spend its latency budget on linearizable money movement and relax consistency only where a customer or an analyst can tolerate what the relaxed model permits.
